title: Red nodule on the face with “spontaneous” regression*
content:
Pseudolymphomatous folliculitis is a rare entity included among the cutaneous pseudolymphomas. A 32-year-old man, with an unremarkable medical history, presented with a two-month history of an asymptomatic solitary nodule on his left cheek. Histopathological examination demonstrated a dense nodular and diffuse dermal lymphocytic infiltrate with numerous histiocytes and dendritic cells that surrounded hypertrophic hair follicles. Pseudolymphomatous folliculitis commonly presents in the fourth decade of life, with no sex predominance, as an asymptomatic, rapidly growing and solitary red dome-shaped nodule on the face. It has a benign clinical course as the lesions usually resolve with surgical excision or regress spontaneously after incisional biopsy. Although there is no report of pseudolymphomatous folliculitis progressing into lymphoma in the literature, follow-up of these patients is recommended.

INTRODUCTIONPseudolymphomatous folliculitis (PLF) is a rare entity included among the cutaneous pseudolymphomas or cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasias. Since its description in 1986 by McNutt, less than 50 cases have been reported in the literature, most of them in Japan.1CASE REPORTA 32-year-old man, with an unremarkable medical history, presented with a two-month history of an asymptomatic solitary nodule on his left cheek. The patient was otherwise well, without systemic symptoms, and he denied history of trauma, sun exposure or insect bite before the onset of the cutaneous disease.Physical examination revealed a red, dome-shaped and firm nodule of 13x13 mm in size on the left cheek (Figure 1). There was no lymphadenopathy and full skin examination was unremarkable. Figure 1Red, dome-shaped and firm nodule on the left cheek Laboratory studies, including a complete blood analysis with serum lactate dehydrogenase level, beta-2 microglobulin, and serum protein electrophoresis, were all normal or negative.A 4-mm punch biopsy was taken and hematoxylin-eosin (HE) stained sections of the specimen demonstrated a dense nodular and diffuse dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, separated from the epidermis by a grenz zone, and admixed with numerous histiocytes and dendritic cells that surrounded the pilosebaceous units (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining revealed that the infiltrate consisted of a mixed population of CD20-positive B-cells and CD3, CD4 and CD8-positive T-cells, with abundant S100 and CD1a-positive dendritic cells surrounding hair follicles, consistent with the diagnosis of pseudolymphomatous folliculitis (Figures 3 and 4). Clonal T-cell receptor and immunoglobulin heavy chain gene rearrangements were not performed. Figure 2Dense nodular and diffuse dermal lymphocytic infiltrate, separated from the epidermis by a grenz zone, and admixed with numerous histiocytes and dendritic cells surrounding the pilosebaceous units. A - Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification x 40. B - Hematoxylin- eosin, original magnification x 100 Figure 3IImmunohistochemical staining. A - CD3. B - CD4. C - CD8 and D - CD20 Figure 4IImmunohistochemical staining. A - S100 e B - CD1a DISCUSSIONPLF commonly presents in the fourth decade of life, with no sex predominance, as an asymptomatic, rapidly growing and solitary red dome-shaped nodule on the face, especially on the nose, cheek, eyelid or forehead.2,3Histologically, it is characterized by a benign proliferation of mixed polyclonal cells surrounding and invading hypertrophic hair follicles. The infiltrate consists of a mixed population of B (CD20+ and CD79a +) and T (CD3+, CD4+ and CD8+) lymphocytes mixed with histiocytes and dendritic cells (S100+ and CD1a+) in varying proportions.1-5T-cell receptor and immunoglobulin heavy chain gene rearrangements have been negative in all cases tested.3,4 However, as atypical lymphocytes can be observed, PLF must be differentiated from primary malignant cutaneous lymphomas by histology and molecular studies. Although there is no report of PLF progressing into lymphoma in the literature, follow-up of these patients is recommended because of the possibility of recurrence.1-5PLF has a benign clinical course as the lesions usually resolve with surgical excision or regress spontaneously after incisional biopsy. This is probably because PLF represents a delayed response to an antigen located in the follicular lumen or epithelium, and the excision or biopsy results in the removal of this antigen3. In our case, within one month of the biopsy, a spontaneous regression of the lesion was observed.Finally, it is important to establish a correct diagnosis to avoid overtreatment of this indolent condition.

diagnosis.diagnosis_raw: Pseudolymphomatous folliculitis (PLF) presenting as an asymptomatic solitary nodule on the left cheek
diagnosis.disease_name: Pseudolymphomatous folliculitis (cutaneous pseudolymphoma / cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia)
diagnosis.severity_description: Benign/indolent cutaneous pseudolymphoma; solitary facial nodule
diagnosis.quality_of_life_impact: Asymptomatic solitary facial nodule; otherwise well without systemic symptoms
diagnosis.lab_values: Laboratory studies (CBC, LDH, beta-2 microglobulin, serum protein electrophoresis) were normal/negative
diagnosis.disease_duration_before_healing: Two-month history before biopsy; regression observed within one month after biopsy
diagnosis.histology: Dense nodular and diffuse dermal lymphocytic infiltrate with grenz zone; mixed B- and T-cells with numerous histiocytes and dendritic cells surrounding pilosebaceous units/hypertrophic hair follicles

treatment.treatments_raw: 4-mm punch biopsy (incisional biopsy) was performed; no other treatment described
treatment.surgery_outcome: Diagnostic biopsy; lesion subsequently regressed within one month
treatment.treatment_stopped_reason: No additional treatment described beyond biopsy

remission_outcome.time_to_remission_raw: Within one month of the biopsy, a spontaneous regression of the lesion was observed
remission_outcome.verification_detail: Clinical observation of regression within one month after punch biopsy; diagnosis established by histopathology and immunohistochemistry
remission_outcome.tumor_response: Spontaneous regression of the cheek nodule after biopsy

pre_illness_state.pre_illness_description: Unremarkable medical history; denied trauma, sun exposure, or insect bite before onset
pre_illness_state.patient_causal_belief: PLF may represent a delayed response to an antigen in the follicular lumen/epithelium; biopsy/excision may remove the antigen (authors' explanation)

validation.statistical_improbability_notes: PLF is described as benign and known to regress after incisional biopsy; regression may be expected rather than statistically extraordinary.
validation.extraction_notes: Condition is not cancer; regression occurred after biopsy, which authors note commonly triggers regression by removing an antigen. Durability/follow-up not provided.

analysis.case_summary: A 32-year-old man developed a solitary red dome-shaped 13×13 mm nodule on the left cheek diagnosed as pseudolymphomatous folliculitis by biopsy and immunohistochemistry. Within one month after the punch biopsy, the lesion regressed spontaneously.
key_healing_factors: Incisional/punch biopsy followed by spontaneous regression (consistent with known PLF behavior)
unique_features: Cutaneous pseudolymphoma (pseudolymphomatous folliculitis) with regression after biopsy; extensive immunohistochemical characterization reported
analysis.analysis_notes: This is a benign dermatologic pseudolymphoma; the term 'spontaneous regression' is used but occurs after biopsy, and is described as typical for PLF.
